title: "Ethics, liability, and the device line: who answers for the note"
subtitle: "AIM-4 · AIM-X · about one hour"
---

::: {.callout-note title="What you'll learn"}
By the end of this chapter you will have:

1. Used a chatbot to draft a clinic note from a made-up visit, improved the
   prompt once, and kept the version you would use again.
2. Read an AI draft against what the patient said, and decided what you would
   sign, what you would change, and what you would do first.
3. Explained why, under current law, the clinician who signs answers for the
   note, and placed a case in the Price, Gerke, and Cohen four-box grid.
4. Said what one randomized study found when a model explained its reasoning,
   and what that means for "explainable AI" as a safeguard.
5. Practised telling a patient, in plain words, what an AI scribe does and who
   is responsible for the note.
:::

**Time.** About 15 to 20 minutes of reading, 40 minutes of doing, and five minutes
of writing at the end. The podcast and the regulatory detail in Go deeper are
optional. Use the chatbot account your school provides (at CU Anschutz,
ChatGPT Edu or Microsoft Copilot); any free chatbot also works, because
everything you type here is made up. There is nothing to install.

## The sentence you did not write

It is the third month of intern year. Your clinic uses an ambient scribe: a
phone app that listens to the visit and drafts the note. Mr. Alvarez, 68, has
atrial fibrillation and takes apixaban. Halfway through the visit he mentions,
almost in passing, that he stopped it two weeks ago because of nosebleeds. You
talk about that for a minute, then move on to his knee. The scribe's draft is
waiting when you get back to the workroom. It is 6:40 in the evening, you have
fourteen notes to sign, and this one reads well.

::: {.ehr-note}
<div class="hdr"><span>Progress note · Internal Medicine Clinic</span><span>Signed 18:47 · Intern (PGY-1)</span></div>
<div class="sec">Subjective</div>
<p>68M with paroxysmal atrial fibrillation (CHA<sub>2</sub>DS<sub>2</sub>-VASc 2), HTN, and right knee OA presents for follow-up. <mark>Continues apixaban 5 mg BID without bleeding complications.</mark> Reports 3 weeks of right knee pain, worse with stairs, no trauma. Denies chest pain, dyspnea, palpitations.</p>
<div class="sec">Assessment and plan</div>
<p>AF, rate controlled: continue apixaban and metoprolol.<br>Right knee OA: trial of acetaminophen; PT referral; RTC 8 weeks.</p>
<div class="foot">Draft generated by ambient documentation. Reviewed and signed by the clinician. <em>Illustrative note for this chapter; synthetic patient; not any vendor's or institution's material.</em></div>

:::

Read the highlighted sentence. This is the kind of error the published studies
of these tools describe. It is not a slip in the transcript. It is a fluent,
believable sentence that says the opposite of what the patient said. In a
pilot at one academic health system, physicians reviewed 356 scribe-drafted
notes. 18% contained an omission, 11.5% contained a made-up statement, and
5.3% contained an error rated as a serious risk if not corrected. 14.9% of all
notes were signed with no edits at all [@pmid:41996389].

Three weeks later Mr. Alvarez is admitted with a stroke. The admitting team
reads your note. Then the hospital's risk manager reads it, and asks you a
question with one answer: *who wrote this sentence?* The note has your name on
it. The waiting room has a sign about "AI-assisted documentation", and the
medical assistant mentions it at check-in. Whether that counts as consent is a
question courts are being asked right now.

Nobody in this scenario has done anything unusual. A tool that is allowed to
be in the room was wrong, and your name is on the result. This chapter is
about that one question: who answers for the note?

If you would rather try first and read after, do Part A of the [Do](#do) now.
It uses Mr. Alvarez's visit. Then come back.

## Why this matters

You will sign a note drafted by software within a year of starting residency,
possibly within a week. UCHealth, a Colorado health system, announced a
systemwide rollout of the Abridge scribe in February 2026 ([press
release](https://www.businesswire.com/news/home/20260224659841/en/UCHealth-Partners-With-Abridge-to-Deploy-Enterprise-Grade-AI-Systemwide-Enhancing-Patient-and-Provider-Experience)).

**It is your job to learn where these tools help your work, and you learn
that by trying.** A scribe is meant to save you time on the note. It is
also the clearest case where your signature goes on what a tool produced.
This chapter is about knowing what you are signing, and being able to explain
that to a colleague, a patient, or a risk manager.

There is little law here. As far as this course could find, no US malpractice
claim involving a clinical AI tool had reached a verdict by September 2026.
There is no rule to memorize. There is one old principle (you sign it, you
answer for it), a way to reason about legal risk, and a few habits that
protect you and your patient.

## How it works

### How a scribe turns a conversation into a note

An ambient scribe does four things in order. Errors can enter at the second
and third steps, and they look different.

::: {.pipeline}
<div class="step"><b>1. Record</b><span>A phone or room microphone records the visit. This is the step that needs the patient's consent.</span></div>
<div class="step"><b>2. Transcribe</b><span>Speech recognition turns the audio into text and tries to tell the speakers apart.</span><em>Errors here: a word misheard, a "no" dropped, a daughter's words put in the patient's mouth.</em></div>
<div class="step"><b>3. Summarize</b><span>A language model reads the transcript and writes a draft note, section by section.</span><em>Errors here: a sentence that was never said, a detail mentioned in passing left out.</em></div>
<div class="step"><b>4. Review and sign</b><span>You edit the draft. Your signature makes every sentence yours.</span></div>
<div class="fine">Illustrative diagram for this chapter, not any vendor's design.</div>
:::

A transcription error often *looks* wrong: an odd word, a drug name that does
not fit. A summarizing error usually looks right, because the model writes
what usually appears in a note like this one. For Mr. Alvarez, the transcript
could have been perfect and the summary could still say what is usual: that
he continues apixaban. So read the draft against what the patient *said*, not
against what sounds like a normal note. The [scribe open
lab](../appendix/open-labs.qmd#hear-it-draft-it-check-it-a-scribe-from-the-inside)
lets you watch each step make its own kind of error.

### You sign it, you answer for it

Malpractice is a type of negligence. To win a negligence case, the person
suing (the **plaintiff**) must prove four things, which lawyers call the four
**elements**. First, that you owed the patient a duty. Second, that you fell
below the **standard of care**, meaning what a reasonably competent physician
in your position would have done. Third, that this failure caused the harm.
Fourth, that the harm was real. The tool is not a defendant in that list. It
is evidence. Under current law, courts measure the *physician* against the
standard of care. They do not measure the AI against anything
[@pmid:31584609; @pmid:38231630].

So "the AI was wrong" is not, by itself, a legal argument. The question a
court will ask is whether *you* should have known better than to rely on the
output, given what you knew at the time [@pmid:38231630]. Suing the vendor
instead is harder than you might expect. Courts have usually treated clinical
software as a service rather than a product. And under the **learned
intermediary doctrine**, a manufacturer's duty to warn runs to the physician,
who stands between the product and the patient. Price, Gerke, and Cohen note
that this may shift as tools become too opaque for a physician to check
([Price, Gerke, and Cohen, 2024](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK613216/)).

The rule that you answer for what you sign is not new. It applied to a note
drafted by a human scribe or a resident. Mr. Alvarez's case would be argued as "the physician
signed a note saying the patient was taking a medication he had told her he
had stopped." Is that below the standard of care at 6:40 p.m. with fourteen
notes to sign? No court has yet answered that question.

### Four boxes

Price, Gerke, and Cohen published a widely used framework
[@pmid:31584609]. It asks two questions. Did the AI's recommendation match the
standard of care? Did the physician follow it? Two yes-or-no questions give
four boxes. Here, "exposure" means how much legal risk the physician carries.

| | **Physician followed the AI** | **Physician overrode the AI** |
|---|---|---|
| **AI matched the standard of care** | A. Good outcome likely. If harm occurs, exposure is low. One open question: can following a correct recommendation you could not explain still create exposure? | C. High exposure. The physician left the standard of care *and* disagreed with a tool that got it right. |
| **AI departed from the standard of care** | B. High exposure. The physician did the nonstandard thing because the machine said so. | D. The physician was right. What risk remains is in the documentation, in hospital policy, and in the fact that the tool stayed in use. |

: The Price, Gerke, and Cohen 2×2. Rows are what the AI said; columns are what the physician did. {#tbl-price}

The uncomfortable box is B. Under current law, the physician who *follows* the
AI into nonstandard care carries the most risk [@pmid:31584609]. Two
experiments asked members of the public, and one also asked physicians. In a
nationally representative sample of 2,000 US adults, physicians who followed
an AI recommendation for standard care were judged less liable than those who
rejected it. Rejecting a *nonstandard* recommendation gave no similar
protection [@pmid:32978285]. A 2026 study found the same pattern
in US and German adults and in German physicians [@pmid:42242875]. The practical lesson: the tool is safest to follow when it
agrees with what you would have done anyway. When it disagrees, you carry the
risk yourself, whichever way you decide.

Where does Mr. Alvarez's note sit? At first, nowhere: the scribe made no
recommendation. But the note *is* a recommendation once signed. "Continue
apixaban" was the plan. It was written on a premise the patient had
contradicted, and you signed it. Which box is that?

### Explanations did not protect against a biased model

A common answer from institutions is "we will require explainable AI." One
randomized study tested that, and in that test it did not protect clinicians
from a biased model. ([The bias and equity
chapter](core-bias-equity.qmd) uses the same study.)

Jabbour and colleagues gave 457 hospitalists, nurse practitioners, and
physician assistants written cases of acute respiratory failure. Baseline
diagnostic accuracy was 73.0%. A standard AI model raised accuracy by 2.9
points; with an image-based explanation of its reasoning, by 4.4 points. A
*systematically biased* model lowered accuracy by 11.3 points. Adding
explanations to the biased model recovered 2.3 points. The confidence interval
for that difference crossed zero, so the true recovery may be nothing
[@pmid:38112814].

![The Jabbour finding, redrawn from the paper's own numbers. Explanations
helped a little when the model was right and did not significantly help when
the model was wrong. Data from Jabbour et al., *JAMA* 2023;330:2275–2284;
figure drawn for this chapter.](../images/jabbour-2023-explanations.svg){#fig-jabbour fig-alt="Bar chart of change in clinician diagnostic accuracy in percentage points from a 73.0% baseline. Standard AI model without explanation plus 2.9; with explanation plus 4.4; biased model without explanation minus 11.3; biased model with explanation minus 9.1. Whiskers show 95% confidence intervals; the two biased-model intervals overlap."}

Apply that to @tbl-price. A defense that says "the tool showed its reasoning,
so the physician should have caught it" must answer this evidence.
**Automation bias** is the habit of trusting a machine's suggestion more than
it deserves. In this study, image-based explanations did not reliably reduce
it.
Automation bias is a property of tired people under time pressure, which is
what you will be at 6:40 p.m.

### The note, the patient, and the contract

Three things follow when an AI tool touches a note, and they are separate.

**The note.** First, read the *plan* against the *conversation*, not against
the draft's own subjective section. The draft agrees with itself even when it
is wrong. If you find an error after signing, add an addendum; do not quietly
edit the signed note. Second, where your institution's policy calls for it,
record that the note was drafted with ambient documentation and reviewed by
you. Many systems add that line automatically. If yours does, know what it
says. It is an **attestation**, a statement in your name that something is
true. A complaint against Sharp HealthCare alleges that the vendor's tool
inserted a statement that the patient "consented" to recording when, the
plaintiff says, no one asked.

**The patient.** Whether the patient knows an AI is in the room is an ethical
question first, and increasingly a legal one. In one academic center's
ambient-documentation pilot, 81.6% of patients consented when given basic
information. That fell to 55.3% when they were told about data storage and the
company involved. Asked who should answer for a documentation error linked to
the tool, 64.1% of patients said the physician [@pmid:40694347].

::: {.press-clips}
<div class="press-clip"><div class="src">KPBS · news</div><a class="hl" href="https://www.kpbs.org/news/health/2025/12/11/lawsuit-claims-sharp-healthcare-secretly-recorded-exam-room-conversations-without-patient-consent">Lawsuit claims Sharp HealthCare secretly recorded exam room conversations without patient consent</a><div class="date">11 December 2025</div></div>
<div class="press-clip"><div class="src">TechTarget · Healthtech Security</div><a class="hl" href="https://www.techtarget.com/healthtechsecurity/news/366641717/Sutter-Health-MemorialCare-face-class-action-lawsuit-over-AI-scribe-use">Sutter Health, MemorialCare face class action lawsuit over AI scribe use</a><div class="date">14 April 2026</div></div>
<div class="press-clip"><div class="src">Becker's Hospital Review</div><a class="hl" href="https://www.beckershospitalreview.com/strategy/ambient-ai-lawsuit-highlights-importance-of-patient-consent/">Ambient AI lawsuit highlights importance of patient consent</a><div class="date">2026</div></div>
:::

These are complaints, not findings, so treat them as allegations. They rely
on California's all-party-consent recording law, its medical-confidentiality
statute, and the federal Wiretap Act. Several states, California among them,
require every party's consent to record a conversation. Whether a waiting-room sign meets
that requirement is what the courts are being asked. This chapter's view: a
conversation with the patient does more than the sign, and [the patient communication
chapter](core-patient-communication.qmd) covers how to have it.

**The contract.** HIPAA, the federal health privacy law, lets a **covered
entity** such as your hospital share protected health information with a
vendor only under a **business associate agreement** (BAA). That contract
makes the vendor legally responsible for protecting the data. An
institution-licensed scribe should run under one; ask. The consumer chatbot on your phone
does not. Which tools are covered, and in which account, is set by your
institution's policy, so check it. At CU Anschutz, for example, ChatGPT Edu
and Microsoft Copilot are covered when you sign in with university
credentials. They are not covered through a personal account. If nobody can tell you in a
sentence whether a tool has a BAA and what the policy allows, the answer is
no.

### The rules, in brief

Much of the regulation is changing. Three points are enough for now; the
full version is optional, in [Go deeper](#the-regulatory-detail-optional).

- **Not every AI tool is a regulated device.** The US Food and Drug
  Administration (FDA) uses four criteria to decide whether software that
  gives clinicians recommendations escapes its review. The fourth usually
  decides: can the clinician check the basis for the advice, with time to do
  so? Your scribe is probably not regulated as decision support, because it
  records and summarizes rather than recommends. If so, FDA does not review
  it, and your review before you sign is the check.
- **Cleared is not validated.** FDA clearance means the manufacturer convinced
  FDA the device is about as safe and effective as something already on the
  market. Of 130 FDA decision summaries for AI devices, about half reported any
  clinical performance data [@pmid:33820998], and a 2024 follow-up found the
  gap persists [@pmid:39187696].
- **The rules change.** FDA's decision-support guidance was replaced twice in
  January 2026. Before you quote any rule, open the primary source and check
  the date at the top.

## Do

Use made-up material only. Mr. Alvarez and his visit are invented. What counts
as patient information, and why taking out the name is not enough: [the
patient information page](../course/patient-information.qmd).

### Part A: draft the note, then decide what you would sign (about 25 minutes)

Here is the conversation from the opening scenario. C is the clinician, P is
Mr. Alvarez.

```{.script}
C: Mr. Alvarez, good to see you. How have things been?
P: Mostly fine. The heart's been quiet. No racing.
C: Any chest pain, or trouble breathing?
P: No. Nothing like that.
C: And you're still taking the apixaban, twice a day?
P: Well, no. I stopped it about two weeks ago. I kept getting nosebleeds.
   One lasted almost an hour.
C: Okay. That's important, and I'm glad you told me.
   Any blood in your urine or your stool?
P: No.
C: We need to sort out the blood thinner. Let me think about the options,
   and we'll come back to it. Now, the knee?
P: The right one. Three weeks now. Worse on stairs. I didn't fall.
   I've been taking naproxen from the drugstore.
C: Let's stop the naproxen. Try acetaminophen instead,
   and I'll send you to physical therapy.
P: Fine by me.
C: Still taking the metoprolol?
P: Every morning.
C: Good. Let's see you back in eight weeks.
```

**1. Get a draft (5 minutes).** Paste the conversation into your chatbot with
this prompt:

```
You are an ambient documentation tool in an outpatient clinic.
Write a SOAP progress note from this visit transcript.
```

Read the draft once, the way you would at 6:40 p.m. Note anything you would
change.

**2. Ask for a better draft (5 minutes).** Start a new chat, paste the
conversation again, and try this:

```
Write a SOAP progress note from this visit transcript, using only what
was said. Do not add anything a typical note would contain unless it is
in the transcript. If the plan for a problem was not stated, write
"Plan not stated" instead of inventing one. After the note, list:
(1) anything you inferred rather than heard, and
(2) anything said in the visit that is not in the note.
```

Compare the two drafts. The second prompt asks the tool to show you where to
look. Its lists can still be wrong, so you still read the whole note.

**3. Decide what you would sign (15 minutes).** Take the better draft. Read
it sentence by sentence against the conversation and mark each sentence:
*said*, *not said*, or *changed*. Then list anything said that the note left
out. Look hardest at three things: the apixaban, the naproxen, and the plan
for anticoagulation. Then edit the draft into the note you would sign.

Your draft may or may not get the apixaban right. Either way, look at the plan.
The clinician said "we'll come back to it" and never did. No draft can make
that decision for you. Decide what you would do about it, and when.

Record this:

```
My drafting prompt (the version I would use again):
__________________________________________________________________

A sentence I changed, added, or deleted before signing, and why:
__________________________________________________________________

What I would do about the apixaban before I sign, and by when:
__________________________________________________________________

My rule for reading a drafted note, in one sentence:
__________________________________________________________________
```

### Part B: explain it to the patient (about 15 minutes)

Mr. Alvarez saw the sign in the waiting room. Practise the conversation. Use
this prompt:

```
Play Mr. Alvarez, a 68-year-old man at a clinic visit. The waiting room
has a sign saying the clinic uses AI-assisted documentation. Ask me,
one at a time: what the phone on the desk is doing, who hears the
recording, and who is responsible if the note gets something wrong.
React as a real patient would. After three questions, step out of the
role and tell me which answer was clear, which was vague, and anything
I said that I may not actually know.
```

Answer in your own words. If you do not know something, such as where the
recording is stored, say so and say who would know. Then write the two or
three sentences you would actually say to a patient. Keep them; you will need
them in July.

## Check

| You have | Meets | Falls short |
|---|---|---|
| Two drafts | A first prompt and a better one, and what changed in the output | One prompt only |
| A line-by-line read | Each sentence marked said, not said, or changed, against the conversation | "It read well" |
| The apixaban decision | What you would write in the plan and do before signing, and by when | Signed as drafted |
| What you would tell the patient | Two or three plain sentences, including who answers for the note, and honesty about what you do not know | Jargon, or a promise you cannot keep |
| A box for the original note | A box of @tbl-price, with the recommendation named | "It depends" |
| Your reading rule | One sentence that would have caught the apixaban error in the original draft | "Read it carefully" |

## What this changes for you

Go back to 6:40 p.m., the original draft, and the stroke three weeks later.
Write three sentences. First, which box of @tbl-price the signed note is in,
and which of the four elements would be hardest for Mr. Alvarez's lawyer to
prove. Second, name one fact that would change your answer if it were
different. Candidates: the time of day, the number of notes, an attestation
line inserted automatically, a clinic policy on reading drafts, or whether
Mr. Alvarez knew the scribe was running. Say which way it changes your answer. Third, what you will do
differently with the fourteenth note.

Then reread the sentence you wrote in [week 1](core-centaur-cyborg.qmd), on
the part of clinical judgment you will not hand over. Would you change it now?
Date both and keep them.

## Summary

- The clinician who signs the note answers for it. The AI is evidence, not a
  defendant. As far as this course could find, no US malpractice claim
  involving a clinical AI tool had reached a verdict by September 2026.
- A summarizing error looks like a normal note. Read the plan against what the
  patient said. Ask the tool to mark what it inferred, and still read it all.
- The riskiest box is following a tool into nonstandard care.
- A biased model cut clinician accuracy by 11 points, and explanations did not
  significantly repair it.
- Tell the patient, know what the attestation says, and know whether there is
  a BAA for the tool.
- Cleared is not validated, and the rules change. Check the date on the source.

## Go deeper

### Papers

- The 2×2 [@pmid:31584609] and the *NEJM* liability analysis [@pmid:38231630],
  read together; then the two juror experiments [@pmid:32978285;
  @pmid:42242875].
- Jabbour in full, including the written cases and the explanation format
  that did not help [@pmid:38112814].
- What scribes get wrong, measured: the academic-system pilot [@pmid:41996389]
  and a comparison of five platforms on simulated visits, where 19.5% of
  transcript errors reached the note and an average of three errors per case
  had potential for moderate-to-severe harm [@pmid:41234546]. A review in
  emergency medicine adds the equity finding. The speech-recognition layer
  under these tools has higher word error rates for Black speakers than for
  White speakers. So the patient most likely to be misdocumented is not
  random [@pmid:42110031].
- Consent as it actually happens in clinic [@pmid:40694347].
- Skill loss after using a tool, called deskilling [@pmid:40816301] (the
  study [the centaur-or-cyborg chapter](core-centaur-cyborg.qmd) uses), and a
  2026 systematic review of automation bias and deskilling with generative
  tools [@pmid:42445869].
- Cleared is not validated [@pmid:33820998; @pmid:39187696].
- The National Academy of Medicine's AI Code of Conduct, discussion draft
  [@pmid:39830818] and the informatics community's commentary on it
  [@pmid:39658328]; the 2025 final is a NAM publication.
- Eight guiding principles for AI tools in health care
  [@doi:10.1038/s43856-023-00279-9], a useful checklist for any tool your
  institution adopts. Also in [the appraisal chapter](core-appraisal.qmd).

### The regulatory detail (optional)

About 15 minutes. Everything here was current in early September 2026, and
much of it will change.

**Where a tool becomes a medical device.** Software that gives clinicians
recommendations is either a medical device, regulated by FDA, or it is not.
The law draws the line with four **criteria** (section 520(o)(1)(E) of the
Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act). Software counts as **non-device clinical
decision support** (non-device CDS), and so avoids FDA review, only if it
meets all four:

1. It is **not** intended to acquire, process, or analyze a medical image, a
   signal from a lab test (an in vitro diagnostic), or a signal from a
   monitor.
2. It is intended to display, analyze, or print medical information.
3. It is intended to *support or provide recommendations* to a health care
   professional about prevention, diagnosis, or treatment.
4. It is intended to let that professional **independently review the
   basis** for the recommendation, so that they do not rely mainly on it to
   make the decision for a patient.

Criterion 4 decides most real cases. A risk score with no visible reasoning
fails it. The same score may pass if it shows its inputs, its logic, and the
validation behind it, in plain language. In the current guidance, FDA says
that software meant for a time-critical decision does not meet criterion 4,
because the clinician will not have time to review the basis. FDA names
automation bias as the reason ([FDA, Clinical Decision Support Software,
guidance issued January 29,
2026](https://www.fda.gov/regulatory-information/search-fda-guidance-documents/clinical-decision-support-software)).

```{mermaid}
%%| label: fig-cds-path
%%| fig-alt: "Flowchart of the four criteria as yes-or-no questions. Analyzes an image or signal: yes leads to device. Displays or analyzes medical information: no leads to device. Supports or provides recommendations to a clinician: no leads to device. Clinician can independently review the basis with time to do so: no leads to device, yes leads to non-device CDS with no FDA review."
%%| fig-cap: "The four criteria as a path. Any 'no' makes the software a device. Criterion 4 is where most real tools are decided. It is a question about what the clinician can see, not about how accurate the model is."
flowchart TD
  accTitle: The four criteria as a path
  accDescr: Flowchart of the four criteria as yes-or-no questions. Analyzes an image or signal, yes leads to device. Displays or analyzes medical information, no leads to device. Supports or provides recommendations to a clinician, no leads to device. Clinician can independently review the basis with time to do so, no leads to device, yes leads to non-device CDS with no FDA review.
  q1{"Does it analyze an image,<br/>an IVD signal, or a signal<br/>from a monitor?"} -- yes --> dev[Device: FDA oversight]
  q1 -- no --> q2{"Does it display or analyze<br/>medical information?"}
  q2 -- no --> dev
  q2 -- yes --> q3{"Does it support or provide<br/>recommendations to a clinician?"}
  q3 -- "no (directs the decision,<br/>or is patient-facing)" --> dev
  q3 -- yes --> q4{"Can the clinician independently<br/>review the basis, with time to do so?"}
  q4 -- "no (black box,<br/>or time-critical)" --> dev
  q4 -- yes --> nd[Non-device CDS:<br/>no FDA review]
```

A sepsis alert that fires from vital-sign trends is a device. It fails
criterion 1 (it processes monitor signals) and probably criterion 4 (it is
time-critical). Any tool that reads an image is a device on criterion 1 alone,
which is why most of the AI devices on FDA's list are radiology tools. A tool
that matches a diagnosis to a guideline and shows you the guideline is
non-device CDS. A large language model that answers a clinical question in
fluent prose, with no visible source, is a harder case. FDA has not yet said
which it is. The criteria are for software that supports clinical decisions.
A scribe that records and summarizes, without recommending, is probably
outside them, but check FDA's current position before you rely on that. In
August 2026 the agency
published a discussion paper on generative-AI-enabled devices. It names
hallucination, meaning made-up content stated as fact, as the property that
sets these tools apart, and asks for comment by 19 October 2026. A discussion
paper is not guidance ([FDA, *Considerations for the Regulation of Generative
AI-Enabled Medical Devices*, August 18,
2026](https://www.fda.gov/medical-devices/digital-health-center-excellence/considerations-regulation-generative-ai-enabled-medical-devices-discussion-paper-and-request)).

::: {.callout-important title="This guidance was replaced twice while the course was being written"}
The four criteria come from a 2016 statute. FDA's guidance on them was issued
in September 2022, replaced on January 6, 2026, and replaced again on
January 29, 2026. The January 29 version is the one linked above. The
January revisions were presented as a loosening of the rules. The main real
change is that FDA will now accept a tool that gives a *single*
recommendation, where only one is clinically appropriate, instead of
insisting on a list. The four criteria themselves did not change. Before you
rely on anything in this section, open the FDA page and check the date at
the top.
:::

**A model that changes.** FDA **clearance** is permission to sell a specific
version of a specific algorithm, and most modern models are updated all the
time. FDA's answer, made final in December 2024, is the **Predetermined
Change Control Plan** (PCCP). In the original submission, the manufacturer
describes the changes it expects to make, the steps it will follow to make and
test them, and what effect it expects them to have. Updates that fall inside
the plan do not trigger a new review
([FDA, PCCP guidance, final, December 4,
2024](https://www.fda.gov/regulatory-information/search-fda-guidance-documents/marketing-submission-recommendations-predetermined-change-control-plan-artificial-intelligence)).
The question to ask any vendor: if the model on my unit today is not the
model that was cleared, what did clearance tell me?

::: {.callout-note title="Your right to see inside the EHR's tools: status as of September 2026"}
[The appraisal chapter](core-appraisal.qmd) said you have something close to
a legal right to see how a decision-support tool inside your EHR was built and
tested. The federal HTI-1 rule (2024) requires certified EHRs to show "source
attributes" for predictive decision-support tools: what they were trained on,
how they were validated, whether fairness was tested. **It is in force.**
Developers began collecting a year of real-world performance data in January
2026. But in January 2026 the same office proposed a rule to loosen this,
called HTI-5. It would remove the "model card" source-attribute requirements
entirely. The stated reason is that clinicians rarely opened them. The comment
period closed on 27 February 2026. As of this writing, HTI-5 has not been
finalized ([ASTP/ONC, HTI-5 proposed
rule](https://www.healthit.gov/topic/laws-regulation-and-policy/hti-5-proposed-rule-fact-sheet)).
So the right exists today and may not next year.
:::

**Rules elsewhere.** Under the European Union's AI Act, software that is
already a regulated medical device automatically counts as **high-risk**,
which brings extra duties for risk management, data governance, human
oversight, and record-keeping. Those duties were due to apply in August 2026.
In July 2026, under a "Digital Omnibus" amendment, they were delayed: to
December 2027 for standalone high-risk systems, and to August 2028 for AI
built into regulated products, which is where medical devices sit
([Regulation (EU) 2026/1744; see the Orrick summary, July
2026](https://www.orrick.com/en/Insights/2026/07/EU-AI-Act-Update-Digital-Omnibus-Finalizes-8-Compliance-Changes)).
Over the same period, the United States withdrew its 2023 executive order on
AI safety, loosened rules at both FDA and ONC, and tried, so far without a
statute, to override state AI laws.

::: {.callout-note title="Your insurer, briefly"}
Malpractice insurers have not written AI out of their policies. The chief
operating officer of The Doctors Company told Medical Economics in 2025 that
the carrier has no AI exclusion, and that it would defend a physician and pay a
covered claim when AI played a role
([interview](https://www.medicaleconomics.com/view/ai-on-trial-how-malpractice-insurers-can-help-physicians-navigate-new-risks)).
The carrier reprinted the interview in its own newsletter. Across the wider
market, insurers decide case by case, and they advise physicians to tell
their insurer before adopting a clinical AI tool
[VERIFY: quote against the Medical Economics interview; the carrier's site links it but does not repeat the wording; checked 2026-09-08]{.verify}.
For a resident, the coverage that matters first is your institution's.
Someone in the GME office can tell you what it says. Ask in orientation, not
after.
:::

**Optional exercise: has it changed? (about 15 minutes).** Pick one question.
Find the current answer from the primary source: the agency, the statute, the
court docket (the court's own record of a case), or the organization's own
page. Record the URL, the date you checked, and the date shown on the source.
A chatbot can help you find the document, but the answer must come from the
document itself.

1. What is the issue date on FDA's current Clinical Decision Support Software
   guidance, and do the four criteria still read as listed above?
2. Has ONC finalized HTI-5? If so, does the "model card" requirement still
   exist?
3. Has FDA issued generative-AI guidance (not a discussion paper) for
   AI-enabled devices?
4. Has any US malpractice claim involving a clinical AI tool reached a
   verdict?
5. Does your own institution have a written policy on ambient documentation,
   on consent for it, and on which AI tools carry a business associate
   agreement? Find the document, or record who told you none exists.

### Primary sources to bookmark

Check the date on each before quoting it.

- [FDA, Clinical Decision Support Software](https://www.fda.gov/regulatory-information/search-fda-guidance-documents/clinical-decision-support-software)
- [FDA, AI-enabled medical devices list](https://www.fda.gov/medical-devices/software-medical-device-samd/artificial-intelligence-enabled-medical-devices).
  1,614 authorizations at the 4 September 2026 update; 335 decisions in 2025, a
  record year; about three quarters in radiology. The FDA says the list is not
  complete, so re-count from its CSV and give the date when you quote it.
- [ASTP/ONC, HTI-1 and HTI-5](https://www.healthit.gov/topic/laws-regulation-and-policy/hti-5-proposed-rule-fact-sheet)
- [HHS, business associate contracts](https://www.hhs.gov/hipaa/for-professionals/covered-entities/sample-business-associate-agreement-provisions/index.html)
